tasks.intent: Show me the distribution of GDP per capita across all countries in 2022 so I can see how skewed global income is.

data.description: GDP per capita, PPP (constant 2017 international dollars) for every country in a single year, one value per country.

expected.chart_family: histogram (with a considered bin width; a log-scaled x-axis or an accompanying ECDF is defensible given the heavy right skew)
expected.key_insight: The distribution is strongly right-skewed: most countries cluster at low-to-middle income with a long thin tail of rich outliers, so the mean sits well above the median.

failure_modes: Plotting a sorted bar chart of every country instead of binning into a histogram, so the reader sees a ranking rather than the shape and spread of the distribution.
Choosing an arbitrary default bin count (Sturges on a skewed variable) that either over-smooths the tail into one giant bar or shatters the peak into noise, misrepresenting modality.
Truncating the x-axis to exclude high-income outliers, hiding the long right tail that is the entire point of the figure.
Encoding frequency with a rainbow fill across bins, implying an ordered categorical meaning to bar color where only bar height (a position/length judgment) carries information.
Reporting only the mean with a vertical line and omitting the median, so the reader cannot see that skew pulls the two apart.

tasks.intent: Compare the distribution of adult body mass index across a handful of OECD countries — I want to see which populations are shifting heavier, not just the average.

data.description: Age-standardized distribution of mean adult BMI by country; per-country summary statistics (median and quantiles) suitable for a boxplot or the underlying survey microdata for a violin/ridgeline.

expected.chart_family: small-multiple ridgeline (or horizontal boxplots / violins) with countries sorted by median BMI
expected.key_insight: Populations differ not just in central BMI but in spread and right-tail thickness; some countries have shifted the whole distribution rightward while others have fattened only the upper tail.

failure_modes: Reducing each country to a single mean bar, discarding spread and tail shape and defeating the explicit request to see the distribution rather than the average.

Leaving the countries in alphabetical or data-file order instead of sorting by median, so the reader cannot perceive the ranking or the systematic shift across the group (violates the ordering principle for comparison).
Assigning each country a saturated hue from a categorical rainbow when the countries form an ordered sequence by median, wasting the color channel and adding visual noise.
Overlapping violins or boxes so densely that their outlines collide, destroying the figure-ground separation that lets each distribution be read individually.
Drawing boxplots without indicating sample size or overlaying the raw points, so the reader cannot judge whether tail differences are real or artifacts of thin data.

tasks.intent: Plot the distribution of daily maximum temperatures at a US city for the last 30 years so I can see how spread out summer heat is and how heavy the extreme-heat tail is.

data.description: Daily maximum temperature observations for a single station aggregated to the summer months across three decades; one temperature value per day.

expected.chart_family: histogram or kernel-density plot, with an ECDF as a strong alternative for reading tail probabilities precisely
expected.key_insight: The temperature distribution is roughly unimodal but has a noticeably fat upper tail, so extreme-heat days occur far more often than a normal fit would predict.

failure_modes: Drawing a time series line over 30 years instead of a distribution, answering a trend question the user did not ask and hiding the shape and spread entirely.
Using a bin width so coarse that the fat upper tail is absorbed into the modal bar, erasing exactly the extreme-heat signal the user wants to see.
Filling the density curve with a red-to-blue diverging ramp keyed to temperature, implying a meaningful zero/midpoint on a channel (fill hue) that carries no quantitative value here.
Overlaying a smooth normal-curve fit without noting the tail departure, leading the reader to believe extreme days are rarer than the empirical data shows.
Starting the count axis above zero so bar heights are no longer proportional to frequency, exaggerating differences between bins (a length-judgment violation).

tasks.intent: Show the age distribution of the US population in 2020 — I want to see the shape of the age structure, the baby-boom bulge and the younger cohorts.

data.description: Resident population counts by single-year or five-year age band from the 2020 Census, optionally split by sex for a population pyramid.
data.shape: 18 five-year age bands x 1 count (or x 2 sexes)

expected.chart_family: histogram over ordered age bands (or a back-to-back population pyramid if split by sex)
expected.key_insight: The age structure is no longer a clean pyramid: cohort bulges (the baby boom now in older bands) and a narrowing base reveal a maturing, near-stationary population.

failure_modes: Rendering the age bands as a pie or donut, forcing angle/area comparisons across an inherently ordered quantitative axis where adjacency and position carry the meaning.
Reordering age bands by population size instead of keeping them in natural age order, destroying the readable shape of the age structure.
Adding gaps between bars so the histogram reads as unrelated categories, breaking the contiguity that signals a continuous binned variable.
On a sex-split pyramid, using two arbitrary categorical hues with poor luminance contrast rather than a clear paired encoding, making the male/female comparison hard to read at a glance.
3-D extruded bars that distort height-to-count proportionality through perspective, corrupting the length judgment the chart depends on.

tasks.intent: Give me the distribution of internet download speeds across countries in 2023 so I can see the global spread and how long the tail of fast-broadband nations is.

data.description: Median fixed-broadband download speed per country for a single year, one value per country.

expected.chart_family: histogram (log x-axis or a companion ECDF is defensible given the right skew across two orders of magnitude)
expected.key_insight: Broadband speed is right-skewed across a wide range: a dense cluster of slow-to-moderate countries and a thin tail of very fast nations, so median lags the mean substantially.

failure_modes: Drawing a choropleth map instead of a distribution, which answers 'where' but not the requested 'how spread out and how long is the tail', and buries small fast countries under large slow landmasses.
Binning on a linear axis when the data span two orders of magnitude, so nearly every country falls in the first bin and the fast tail becomes invisible.
Sorting countries into a long ranked bar chart, which shows order but forces the reader to reconstruct the distribution mentally rather than reading its shape directly.
Coloring bins with a spectral rainbow that has non-monotonic perceived luminance, so bar fills read as a false ordinal scale competing with the real height encoding.
Omitting axis labels and units (Mbps) and a clear count axis, leaving the spread uninterpretable and violating the requirement that quantitative axes be honestly and fully labeled.
